prize_parts.citation: For an uncompromising body of fiction that dissolves ordinary psychology, space and causality into dream logic and reinvents the perception of narrative in Chinese.

statement.case_for: Can Xue remains my first choice after reading the colleagues' openings. The case rests on distinctiveness of voice and on formal achievement. Her fiction (Frontier; Love in the New Millennium, as named on the list) replaces realist psychology and causal plot with a dream logic that is held consistently across decades, and it does not depend on a national-allegory or testimonial frame. The project has imaginative and intellectual depth, and her critical writing on other authors supports that. The colleagues' openings place her first or second on all six ballots. I do not treat that convergence as literary evidence. It does mean the main objections can be tested directly in discussion. A single-writer citation is clean, because the contribution is a personal narrative method rather than a movement or a set of political circumstances.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the quality of her prose and the claim of sustained quality over a very large output cannot be confirmed from translation. I cannot judge the Chinese original, and corpus coverage in translation is partial. A consistent method could also mean a narrow range, so the question is whether the later work deepens or only repeats the earlier work. Several colleagues raise this point, and I cannot dismiss it from public knowledge alone. If the committee cannot answer it with confidence, Cărtărescu or Carson would be the better-grounded recommendation.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for a visionary, densely patterned prose with unusual coherence across volumes and across prose and poetry. She ranks Can Xue second and asks whether the dream-logic method varies enough over the whole oeuvre.
responses.response: I take the coherence argument seriously, and it is why I keep Cărtărescu as my first alternative. I disagree on one point. The reservation about method versus variety applies to him as well, since the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid are long books whose motifs may recur and whose Romanian register translation may flatten. For Can Xue, the variety is in the invention within each work, not in a shift of method. Her work is also more compressed, so repetition costs less. I admit that I cannot settle this by reading across the corpus, and Mattson's doubt about the allegorical method sustaining variety is a fair open question rather than one I can answer.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Zurita first, for long poetic sequences (Purgatory, Anteparadise) that turn collective suffering under the Chilean dictatorship into memorial form, with a fit to the idealist direction of the will that rests on depth rather than political symbolism.
responses.response: I ranked Zurita eighth and I want to qualify that position. His ambition and formal singularity are real, and Olsson is right to insist that the case rest on the poetry and not on the history. My hesitation is practical. Poetry depends most on the original language, and I can only reach partial translated selections. A significant part of the work's force also lies in landscape-scale interventions outside the book, which makes it harder to say what a citation of the written oeuvre would honour. I would want to hear from colleagues who read Spanish before treating the case as secure. Olsson's argument does not change my ranking, but it raises my uncertainty about my own judgment of poetry in translation.

responses.point: Carlberg also puts Can Xue first, as a rigorously maintained dream logic in which formal achievement is original rather than decorative, and she notes her critical writing and the risk that dense, abstract prose loses texture in translation.
responses.response: I agree that the rigor separates the work from decorative surrealism, and I think that distinction carries the case. I would rely on the fiction for the citation and treat the criticism as supporting evidence. Carlberg's translation point is the one I cannot dispel. Agreement between us is not a check on it, because we are reading the same translated sample. I would want the committee to ask directly whether the translations of the longer works carry the voice.

responses.point: Sward ranks Marilynne Robinson second, for meditative, morally serious prose with a recognizable cadence and high consistency across a compact set of novels, with essays extending the project.
responses.response: Robinson's sentence-level control and the coherence of the Gilead sequence are real achievements, and I place her sixth for reasons of breadth and not of quality. A small fiction oeuvre set in one deeply explored world seems a narrower claim than a method that reinvents narrative perception, although a narrower claim is not a lesser one on every criterion. Sward's own caution that acclaim in English should not stand in for a judgement of formal achievement applies equally to the candidates I favour, and I accept it.

uncertainties: I cannot assess Can Xue's Chinese prose directly, and how far the translated voice matches the original is unresolved.
Corpus coverage in English and other major languages is partial, so sustained quality across the full output is not verified.
Whether a very consistent dream-logic method deepens over time or repeats remains open and is raised by several colleagues.
I have not read the works independently, and my judgments of the Spanish, Arabic and Romanian poetry and prose rest on translated selections and public knowledge.
Whether landscape-scale and book-object works (Zurita, Carson) should count within the literary framework of Nobel's will is undecided.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My work on Selma Lagerlöf and my own fiction are context only, and no listed candidate has a documented professional tie to me.
